The slate quarry above Llanfair Uchaf opened in 1798 and at its peak in 1882 employed 1,240 men. Blocks were lowered down a series of 7 inclines to the mill, where they were split by hand into slates as thin as 1/4 inch.
A good splitter could produce 700 roofing slates in a day. The work was paid by the "bargain", a section of rock let to a team of 4 or 5 men each month.
The last block was raised in 1969. Today the inclines form part of a 6 km waymarked trail.

Caisteal Dubh stands on a rocky promontory 30 m above the loch. Built in the late 1400s, it was a stronghold of the MacRuaraidhs until 1746, when government troops burnt the roof and garrisoned the tower for 6 years.
The walls are up to 2.4 m thick at the base. A narrow stair in the north-east corner still climbs to the second floor, but visitors are asked not to go beyond the rope.
The site is open daily from April to October, 10:00 to 17:00. Admission is free.

The pine marten was almost lost from Britain by the 1920s, surviving only in the remote north-west Highlands. Since then it has spread back across much of Scotland, and a small population was released in mid-Wales between 2015 and 2017.
Martens weigh 1.5 to 2.2 kg and are mostly active at dusk. In this forest you are most likely to see one at the feeding table by Hide 2, between 9pm and 11pm in June and July.

The Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act of 1886 gave crofters security of tenure, fair rents and the right to compensation for improvements. It followed years of unrest, including the "Battle of the Braes" on Skye in 1882.
Most crofts are small, often 2 to 5 hectares of in-bye land with a share in the common grazing on the hill. Today there are about 21,000 crofts, home to some 33,000 people.

Gaelic place names describe the land. Beinn means a mountain, often a rounded one, while sgùrr is a steep, rocky peak. Allt is a burn, loch a lake and eilean an island.
Colours appear everywhere: dubh (black), bàn (white or fair), ruadh (red), glas (grey-green) and buidhe (yellow). So Eilean Glas is the grey-green island and Allt Dubh the black burn.
On the map of this area, about 4 in every 5 names are Gaelic in origin.

At Allt Dubh we mash 1.2 tonnes of malted barley at a time, mixed with hot water at 63.5 °C. The sweet liquid, called wort, is cooled and pumped to one of 6 wooden washbacks.
Fermentation takes 72 hours and produces a wash of about 8% alcohol. It is then distilled twice, first in the 8,000-litre wash still and then in the smaller spirit still.
Only the middle cut, between roughly 72% and 64% abv, is kept and filled into casks.

St Tudno's Church was rebuilt in 1867 on the site of a medieval chapel, reusing the 14th-century font and part of the east wall. The bell, cast in 1712, hangs in a small double bellcote above the west door.
Inside, look for the memorial to the 23 men of the parish who died in the First World War, and the window of 1921 showing St Tudno with a coracle.
The church is open daily from 9am until dusk. Donations towards its upkeep, which costs over £7,500 a year, are gratefully received.

At the height of the herring boom in 1907, more than 1,000 boats fished from the ports of the north and east coasts, and the harbour at Port Ruadh handled up to 40,000 barrels a season.
The fish were gutted and packed by teams of 3 women, two gutters and one packer, who followed the fleet from Shetland to Yarmouth. A skilled gutter could clean 60 herring a minute.
By 1950 the shoals had moved and the curing yards stood empty.

Llyn Arian reservoir was completed in 1904 to supply water to the towns of the coast, 74 miles away. The dam is 44 m high and 357 m long, built of local stone by a workforce that reached 1,400 at its peak.
The reservoir holds about 9,100 million litres. Water flows to the coast entirely by gravity, falling 52 m over the length of the aqueduct.
Remains of the navvies' village, including the foundations of the school and hospital, can be seen beside the lower car park.

Golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos)
Length 75–90 cm; wingspan 1.9–2.3 m. Dark brown with a golden-buff nape. Young birds show white patches in the wings and a white tail with a black band.
Scotland holds about 508 pairs (2015 survey), mostly in the Highlands and Islands. Nests, called eyries, are on crags or in old Scots pines, and 1 or 2 eggs are laid in March or April.
Compare the white-tailed eagle, which is larger, with a short, wedge-shaped white tail as an adult.

My grandmother cooked on a range that burned peat, and she never once weighed anything. When I asked how much oatmeal went into her oatcakes, she said "enough", and when I pressed her, "about a cupful, more or less".
The recipes in this book are my attempt to pin those quantities down. I have tested each one at least 3 times, and I give oven temperatures for fan, conventional and gas.
Where a recipe calls for 1 tsp of bicarbonate of soda, please measure it level; a heaped spoon will make your scones taste soapy.

The Strathcullen branch opened on 1 June 1891, linking the glen to the main line at Dunvarran, 18 miles away. At first there were 4 trains each way on weekdays, and a return fare cost 1s 9d.
Passenger services ended in 1960, but goods traffic, mostly timber and sheep, continued until 1964.
The station building at Strathcullen survives as the village hall. A 3 km stretch of the old trackbed between the hall and the viaduct is now a level path suitable for wheelchairs.
